observations.quote: The Duty of Natures Minister, the Physitian.
observations.what: The Duty of Natures Minister, the Physitian
observations.note: The chapter is headed as one thing: the duty of the physician, who is called Natures Minister.

observations.name: P. Ramus
observations.quote: ALL common Philosophy was not bound up in Aaistotle, as P. Ramus hath soundly proved
observations.note: Ramus is named as having proved that common philosophy is not confined to Aristotle; no words of his are given.

observations.quote: nor was the whole Light of Nature drawne into Galen and limited in him only, witnesse Paracelsus
observations.note: The Light of Nature is not confined to Galen; Paracelsus is called as witness, no words of his given.

observations.quote: the liberty of human ingenuity, that Light of Nature, the power to discern and judge as well as himselfe
observations.note: Three phrases stand in apposition: the liberty of human ingenuity, 'that Light of Nature', the power to discern and judge; no man is to deprive another of it.

observations.quote: the Grecian Monarchy is at an end
observations.note: A figure after the naming of Aristotle and Galen. Interpreted (inference from the sentences before it): the rule of the Greek authorities over learning is declared over; the text does not say so in plain words.

observations.quote: he that would be an Excellent Physitian he must be free from every kind of Sect.
observations.note: The excellent physician belongs to no sect.

observations.quote: no man can be said to be truly and throughly learned who is bound up to the rudiments of any one faculty only
observations.note: The reason given in the parenthesis: being bound to one faculty's rudiments is not true learning.

observations.quote: not to be tyed. to the opinion of any one Author, but to follow the naked Truth, and subscribe to it alone
observations.note: The physician follows no single author but the naked Truth alone.

observations.name: Horace
observations.quote: I think and judge as cause I finde
observations.note: The couplet is given as 'that of Horace' (end of CH5.1): judgement by one's own finding, not by another's mind.

observations.name: Horace
observations.quote: Nutlius addictus jurare in verba magistri.
observations.note: The margin gives Latin lines beside the couplet given to Horace; the note itself names no one.

observations.quote: Not that other mens inventions are altogether to be slighted, by stickling onely for one sect
observations.note: Freedom from sects is not to mean slighting what others have found; this qualifies CH5.1.

observations.name: Picus Mirandula
observations.quote: all sects, be they never so many, may well be admitted, because in every one of them there is some thing excellent which is not common to another
observations.note: The saying that every sect holds something excellent of its own is given to Picus Mirandula ('as said that most noble and wise Picus Mirandula').

observations.quote: that most noble and wise Picus Mirandula the Phaenix of Phylosophers
observations.note: Picus Mirandula is set apart with titles of praise.

observations.quote: There is no book so base and bad but hath some good in it which the best Authors have somtimes let slip without taking notice of it.
observations.note: Every book has some good in it that the best authors have missed. B left the voice open; the attribution to Picus closes the sentence before, and nothing in this one gives it to another, so it is ruled CROLL.

observations.name: Fabius
observations.quote: This latter age, saith Fabius, hath endeavored to make the former more compleat
observations.note: Fabius is quoted: the later age completes the former. Where his words end is not marked.

observations.quote: many loathsome errours of the Heathen have been as by a second song
observations.note: Errors of the Heathen are said to have been wiped away by wiser men coming later; 'as by a second song' is a figure the text does not explain. It may still be Fabius's words.

observations.quote: All Secret are by divine Ordination to be discovered.
observations.note: The margin states that all secrets are ordained by God to be discovered.

observations.quote: Doubtlesse there are more secrets yet concealed in the Treasures of Wisdome and Nature then we perceive
observations.note: More secrets remain concealed than are perceived.

observations.quote: are to be sought out by wise-hearted men
observations.note: The concealed secrets are ordained 'for Times and Nations, by an immutable decree' and are to be sought out by 'wise-hearted men'.

observations.quote: Nature certainly, being Circularly, can hardly be wholly comprehended by any mortall man by reason of the shortnesse of his life.
observations.note: No mortal can wholly comprehend Nature, life being short. What 'being Circularly' means is not said in the lines given.

observations.quote: neither the Physick of the Ancients, nor that of Theophrastus, is totally to be rejected
observations.note: Neither the ancients' physick nor Theophrastus's is to be wholly rejected.

observations.quote: nor yet so to be imbraced but that if there be a better found out it also is to be received
observations.note: Nor is either to be embraced so as to shut out something better found later.

observations.quote: both should be compared together, what is best in both let that be cetained
observations.note: The two are to be compared and the best of both kept.

observations.quote: For being but men, they have their failings, in some places they mistake, in other they write one thing contrary to another
observations.note: The authors, being men, err and contradict one another and themselves; 'they' follows the naming of the Ancients and Theophrastus.

observations.quote: The holy Spirit alone hath the plenary or full knowledge of all things, who distributeth to every man according to his particular measure
observations.note: Full knowledge is the holy Spirit's alone; each man receives a measure.

observations.quote: reserving many things to himselfe that we might alway acknowledge him to be our only teacher
observations.note: The holy Spirit holds many things back, so that he be acknowledged the only teacher.

observations.quote: A true Phisitian should be the minister, not a master to Nature
observations.note: The physician serves Nature and does not master it; this takes up the chapter's heading.

observations.name: Hippocrates & Galen
observations.quote: a Philosopher skilfull to cure acording to the conclusion of Hippocrates & Galen
observations.note: That the physician be a philosopher skilful to cure is given as the conclusion of Hippocrates and Galen.

observations.quote: some after the Vulgar manner will be looking below the Moon after the Elementary Nature of things
observations.note: One kind of the 'severall sects of Phylosophers' is set apart: those who look below the Moon at the elementary nature of things.

observations.quote: others far more excellent and more truly deserving the name of Philosophers investigate the Arcana and more secret things of Nature
observations.note: The second kind search out Nature's Arcana and more secret things, and more truly deserve the name of philosopher.

observations.quote: they go into the very inner roomes and Sanctuary of Nature
observations.note: Nature is spoken of as a house with inner rooms and a sanctuary: a figure for the secret things just named.

observations.quote: have the true knowledge and Expeeience of Nature's Light, which maketh a true Physitian indeed
observations.note: Knowledge and experience of Nature's Light is what makes a true physician.

observations.quote: A Physitian is compleated by 3 things
observations.what: 3 things by which a Physitian is compleated
observations.note: Three things are announced; the list names the natural innate virtue of growing things, the celestial influence causing it, its uniting by Chymistry with the firmament, and then the physician's dexterity 'mediating the same' (a word with a gap). Whether that last is a fourth item the wording does not settle.

observations.quote: the uniting of it by Chymistry with the Constellation of the firmament
observations.note: A step of work: the innate virtue of earthly growths is united by Chymistry with the constellation of the firmament. How is not said in these lines.

observations.quote: Many errours of the Ancients are discovered by dayly experience, which yet hath not attained its end neither.
observations.note: Daily experience uncovers the ancients' errors and is itself not yet at its end.

observations.quote: But first, as Paracelsus saith, let him be the legetimate INTERPRETER of NATURE
observations.note: Set in capitals and numbered 'first' (a 'Secondly' follows at CH5.12): the physician's first requirement, to be the interpreter of Nature.

observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.quote: who alone searcheth out its oeconomy, and the universall latitude thereof
observations.note: The words on the interpreter of Nature are given to Paracelsus ('as Paracelsus saith').

observations.quote: prying into all the Species and kinds of all the Creatures that may by themselves be known, and then comes to consider and looke into man
observations.note: The order of inquiry: first all the kinds of creatures, then man.

observations.name: Chirurgia magna
observations.quote: In Chirurgia magna.
observations.note: The margin names a writing beside the words given to Paracelsus.

observations.quote: Phylosophy teacheth the vertues and qualityes of the Earth and Water, as Astronomy doth of the fire and Ayre
observations.note: Phylosophy and Astronomy are told apart by their matter: Earth and Water, fire and Ayre.

observations.quote: Phylosophy and Astronomy make a perfect Phylosopher, not onely in the great, but also in the little world.
observations.note: Both together make the perfect philosopher, in the great and in the little world.

observations.quote: A Physitian should have the knowledge of Phylosophy and Astronomy
observations.note: The physician needs both.

observations.quote: Chyromancy, Pyromancy and Geomancy are the Elements of Astronomy and Phylosophy.
observations.note: Three named arts are called the 'Elements' of Astronomy and Phylosophy; what each is, these lines do not say.

observations.quote: from the knowledge of Heaven and Earth, whose Nature and quality he doth perfectly understand
observations.note: The true philosopher has his origin in knowing Heaven and Earth (the word before the quote holds a gap).

observations.quote: Phylosophy hath i{G148: 1 letter illegible}s Rise and R{G149: 2 letters illegible}t in Admiration.
observations.note: The margin places the rise of Phylosophy in Admiration; two words hold gaps, left as they stand.

observations.quote: Theophrasteans contemplate and admire the workmanship of Nature throughout this mighty frame of the whole Creation
observations.note: A group is named after Theophrastus and described by what it does.

observations.quote: a wise inquisition into the qualities, affections, motions, courses and recourses of the Heavens and fiery bodies
observations.note: Their work, first part: inquiry into the heavens and fiery bodies, their qualities and motions.

observations.quote: lastly into the seeds, principles, dimensions, and instincts of all sublunary bodies
observations.note: Their work, last part: inquiry into the seeds and principles of bodies below the moon.

observations.quote: by which industry and that perpetuall thirst which they have of meditation and cogitation
observations.note: The means named: industry and a constant thirst for meditation and cogitation; prayers and earnest desires are added after the note mark.

observations.quote: By this meditation, which is a frequent cogitation, the manner, cause & reason of every manner of thing is found out.
observations.note: The margin says what meditation is, 'a frequent cogitation', and what it finds out.

observations.quote: they doe at last attaine not onely to understand, but also really to imitate the greatest mysteries and secrets of Nature
observations.note: The Theophrasteans come not only to understand but 'really to imitate' Nature's greatest mysteries and secrets.

observations.quote: that which is more then all, they can tell how to improve and imploy them
observations.note: And, rated above the rest, to improve and employ those secrets.

observations.quote: When the Phylosopher comes to a stand in the Naturall Light of the Macrocosm, then the Physitian begins
observations.note: Where the philosopher stops, the physician begins: the two are set in an order.

observations.quote: to move and proceed in the Analogicall Concordance of the Naturall Light of the Microcosm with that of the great world
observations.note: The physician's field is the 'Analogicall Concordance' between the Natural Light of the Microcosm and that of the great world; 'the great world' stands where 'Macrocosm' stood just before.

observations.quote: Secondly, a Physitian must be a good SPAGIRUS
observations.note: The second numbered requirement, after 'But first' at CH5.8, set in capitals.

observations.quote: one that can seperate the pure from the impure, and restore his Patient to health by a wise Alchymicall preparation
observations.note: The text says what a SPAGIRUS is: one who separates pure from impure and heals by an 'Alchymicall preparation'.

observations.quote: seperate the pure from the impure
observations.note: The step of work named for the SPAGIRUS: separation of pure from impure. No procedure is given in these lines.

observations.quote: restore his Patient to health by a wise Alchymicall preparation
observations.note: Healing is done by an alchymical preparation; what it is, these lines do not say.

observations.quote: As Gold is tryed seven times in the fire, so should a Physitian be
observations.note: A comparison stated by the text: the physician is to be proved by Chymistry as gold is tried in the fire (the next word holds a gap).

observations.quote: Chymistry, which sepereteth the good from the bad
observations.note: Chymistry is described by its work: it separates good from bad.

observations.quote: also he must have somthing of his own Experience confirmed by a diligent inspection into Natures works
observations.note: The physician must also have experience of his own, confirmed by looking into Nature's works.

observations.quote: Phylosophy is a practicall Physicke helping the Physitian to any medicine in a readynesse
observations.note: Phylosophy is here called 'a practicall Physicke'.

observations.quote: he it is who at length becomes a good Physitian, born of the Light of Nature, to whom Nature communicateth his Experience
observations.note: The good physician is 'born of the Light of Nature', and Nature gives him experience.

observations.quote: A Philosopher and Physitian spring one out of another, are the root of each other, the onely Spagyrick cook of all things.
observations.note: Philosopher and physician arise from each other; 'the onely Spagyrick cook of all things' is not explained in the note.

observations.quote: Phylosophy is the mother of Physitians
observations.note: The margin calls Phylosophy the mother of physicians; the rest of the note is broken by gaps.

observations.quote: never was there any man that ever knew and publisht such hard and hidden secrets in all Phylosophy and Physicke
observations.note: Paracelsus is said to have known and published 'hard and hidden secrets' as no one else did.

observations.quote: the true Monarch of Physicke, and first Physitian of man
observations.what: the true Monarch of Physicke, and first Physitian of man
observations.note: Titles of praise given to Paracelsus.

observations.quote: a man and a Phylosopher most worthy of an Eternall Name and honor, whose skill no man ever yet attaind unto, much lesse exceeded
observations.note: Paracelsus judged unequalled and unsurpassed in skill.

observations.quote: whose skill no man ever yet attaind unto, much lesse exceeded
observations.note: Here Paracelsus is beyond reach; at CH5.7 the physick of Theophrastus is not to be so embraced that something better is shut out, and its authors 'have their failings'. Recorded as a difference, not judged.

observations.quote: who alone since Noe's time hath written of the Internall Astrall Man and the service which God created him for
observations.note: Paracelsus alone 'since Noe's time' wrote of the 'Internall Astrall Man'.

observations.quote: as also of the originall both Naturall and Metaphysicall of great and incurable diseases, which none of the former Physitians did ever so much as dream of
observations.note: He also wrote of the natural and metaphysical origin of great and incurable diseases, unknown to earlier physicians.

observations.quote: our Students of Heathenish Phylosophy from whence all errour springeth
observations.note: Heathenish Phylosophy is called the source of all error.

observations.quote: as hath been said, they have taken no notice of that twofold unknown body of the Creatures
observations.note: 'as hath been said' points back to an earlier place in the writing; that place is not among the lines given.

observations.quote: that Mortall, Elementated Physicall and visible Corporeall body of the Elements; and the Astrall Sydereal and invisible of the Firmament and the stars
observations.note: The 'twofold unknown body of the Creatures' is spelled out ('to wit'): a visible body of the Elements and an invisible, astral one of the Firmament and stars.

observations.quote: The Intellectuall Soul of Man, that divine Light flowing out of that spiracle of God and Divine springs pertaineth to the Invisible Phylosophy, whose foundation is CHRIST
observations.note: The Intellectual Soul is called a divine Light out of 'that spiracle of God' and assigned to the Invisible Phylosophy, founded on CHRIST.

observations.quote: All Sciences are perfectly attained unto by the Fundamentall of Faith and new Regeneration or Celestiall Transplantation.
observations.note: All sciences are reached through faith and 'new Regeneration or Celestiall Transplantation' (two names joined by 'or').

observations.quote: Our study therefore and profession of Phylosophy should be Christian-like, not after the manner of the Heathen in hollow empty language and temporaneous Arts
observations.note: Phylosophy is to be Christian, not in the heathen manner of empty language and 'temporaneous Arts'.

observations.quote: Nor are we onely to know all Nature externally and internally, but we are also to make it our onely businesse
observations.note: Knowing all Nature, outwardly and inwardly, is not the whole task; a further 'onely businesse' is named next.

observations.quote: by the supernall help of the Light of Grace we may together with Christ and all the Elect possesse that Eternall Life unto which God hath created us
observations.note: That business: by the Light of Grace to possess eternal life.

observations.quote: this is true Theologicall Phylosophy
observations.note: Knowing Nature and, by the Light of Grace, possessing eternal life is named 'true Theologicall Phylosophy'.

observations.quote: A man cannot have better Phylosophy then f{G162: 1 letter illegible}om God in the Regeneration.
observations.note: The best Phylosophy is had from God in the Regeneration (one word holds a gap, copied as it stands).

observations.quote: Wherefore the New Birth is first to be sought for, and then all other Naturall things will be added without much labour.
observations.note: An order is set: the New Birth first, natural things added after 'without much labour'.

observations.quote: But let us return againe to Theophrastus.
observations.note: The text marks its return to Theophrastus after the passage on Christian philosophy.

observations.quote: He was a man singularly well skild in Chymistry, though he were not the Auther of that Art
observations.note: Paracelsus is skilled in Chymistry but not its first author.

observations.quote: There have been abundance of Phylosophers who have made use of there ingenuity and memory instead of bookes
observations.note: Many philosophers before him worked by ingenuity and memory, not books.

observations.quote: who were famous by that Art before Theophrastus was born, and from whom Paracelsus hath secretly borrowed many things
observations.note: Paracelsus is said to have borrowed 'secretly' from earlier men famous in the art.

observations.quote: from whom Paracelsus hath secretly borrowed many things
observations.note: Here Paracelsus has predecessors famous in the art from whom he borrowed; at CH5.12 none ever knew and published such secrets and none attained his skill. The subjects named differ (Chymistry here; the Astrall Man and the origin of diseases there), so this is recorded as a difference only.

observations.quote: This kind of Phylosophy hath been in good esteem among many Nations.
observations.note: This kind of Phylosophy was esteemed among many nations.

observations.quote: For that noble Pyronomicall Art hath been most ancient
observations.note: The art is given a name and called most ancient; its critics are called 'Dolts and Dunces'.

observations.quote: which heretofore was known only to Kings Princes, & some few of most diligent searchers out of Naturall Phylosophy
observations.note: The art was formerly known to few: kings, princes and some diligent searchers.

observations.quote: which of late hath not been a little improved by that Monarch of Mysteryes Paracelsus
observations.note: A further title for Paracelsus, who is said to have improved the art.

observations.quote: endeavoured to bring to light, restore and amplifie the Ancient doctrine, which by a fatall depravation and neglect of times and men, was lost and obliterated for many years
observations.note: Paracelsus's work is presented as restoring a lost ancient doctrine, by 'the singular providence and impulse of God'.

observations.quote: to wit, the True and Philosophicall Physick which none in his time assayed to restore
observations.note: The 'Ancient doctrine' is named ('to wit'): the True and Philosophicall Physick.

observations.quote: the great obscurity of which art he laboured also to evolve and illustrate
observations.note: The art lies in 'great obscurity', which Paracelsus worked to unfold and make clear.

observations.quote: to purge it from the fucous guile and vizard of imposture
observations.note: He also worked to clear the art of imposture.

observations.quote: to recall the universall consonancy of the Sciences and Muses by a kind of divine copulation from the compasse of the whole circle unto the one only Centre
observations.note: 'by a kind of' marks a figure: the sciences are drawn from the whole circle to one centre. What the Centre is, these lines do not say.

observations.quote: hath stirred up his Emissaries and catch-poles, whom he doth yet dayly egg and set on with a dogged hatred
observations.note: The opposition is laid to the Devil, who stirs up 'Emissaries and catch-poles'.

observations.quote: to keep others from the manger in which they cannot lye themselves
observations.note: A figure for the opponents: they keep others from what they cannot use themselves.

observations.quote: The Physitian that God maketh can doe all things.
observations.note: The physician made by God can do all things.

observations.quote: all wonders, mysteries and secrets are to be attributed to God
observations.note: Wonders, mysteries and secrets come from God, not the Devil, creatures or stars.

observations.name: James 1.17
observations.quote: not to the Devill, Creature, or Stars, James 1.17.
observations.note: The margin cites James 1.17 for ascribing all wonders to God; no words of it are given.

observations.quote: the Author of Physick (from whom as from the Father of Lights is every good and perfect gift)
observations.note: God is called the Author of Physick, to whom the gifts of healing are to be ascribed.

observations.quote: which gifts were bestowed upon Theophrastus, who by peculiar influence was born a Physitian
observations.note: Theophrastus's gifts of curing are God's, and he was 'born a Physitian' by 'peculiar influence'.

observations.name: Emissaries and catch-poles
observations.quote: as though the wicked one were the worker of those cures
observations.note: A view reported in order to be rejected: 'they' (the Emissaries and catch-poles of CH5.14) lay Theophrastus's cures to the Devil, 'like the Pharisees of old'. No words of theirs are given.

observations.quote: thus they make the Devill stonger then the blessed and glorious God, though he be bound fast with the cord of the Omnipotent
observations.note: Croll's answer: this makes the Devil stronger than God, though he is bound and 'deprived of the Light of Grace and Nature'.

observations.quote: Those things are to be ascribed to God alone and to his Law, as to the Author of the whole Universe and of Nature
observations.note: The cures are to be ascribed to God alone and his Law.

observations.quote: the Devill, who hath no power over the Will and Understanding of Man
observations.note: The Devil has no power over man's will and understanding.

observations.quote: by a malicious ignorance obscuring his Wisdome or hidden Image in Man
observations.note: God's Wisdom is also called his 'hidden Image in Man', which the opponents obscure.

observations.quote: to contemn those Secrets which God hath granted to their Nature
observations.note: The German physicians wrong their own country by despising secrets God granted 'to their Nature' and praising only what is foreign.

observations.quote: just as it befell Pet. Ramus from his malicious populer adversaries, because he stopt the current of youthfull studies in the silly, common, and corruptible Phylosophy
observations.note: Pet. Ramus's case is set beside Paracelsus's as a like one.

observations.quote: as the Aristotelians unworthily rose up and set themselves against him, even so doe the mingle mangle Physitians against Theophrastus Paracelsus
observations.note: A parallel: Aristotelians against Ramus, 'mingle mangle Physitians' against Paracelsus.

observations.quote: whose learning is deservedly admired and wondered at by Forraine
observations.note: Paracelsus's learning is admired by foreign nations (the word 'Nations' follows the note mark).

observations.quote: it is impossible for any to imitate him
observations.note: None can imitate what he has written; the sentence's opening words are garbled in the text as given.

observations.name: Paracels.
observations.quote: See Paracels. de Fundamento Sa{G164: 1 letter illegible}ientia.
observations.note: The margin sends the reader to a named writing of Paracelsus and to a second book whose title is broken by gaps.

observations.quote: He that doth not carelesly read but inwardly examine his writings will perceive as much.
observations.note: A direction on how Paracelsus is to be read: not carelessly but examined 'inwardly'.

observations.quote: they blush not also to wrangle against his Divinity, which they have neither seen nor read, nor by reason of their blockishnesse can they understand
observations.note: The opponents also attack Paracelsus's Divinity without having seen or read it.

observations.quote: in Physick as the Soule in the body.
observations.note: Divinity should dwell in Physick as the soul in the body.

observations.quote: he onely is able to judge of Truth who is inspired with Divine Wisdome
observations.note: Only one inspired with Divine Wisdom can judge of Truth, so the opponents cannot judge Paracelsus's Divinity.

observations.quote: he hath successelesly endeavoured to make known to the ingratefull gratefull and unworthy world
observations.note: In his divine writings Paracelsus tried, 'successelesly', to make something known to the world; 'ingratefull gratefull' stands so in the text.

observations.quote: that invincible united Fundamentall of Theologicall and Phylosophicall Truth and perfect Piety
observations.what: that invincible united Fundamentall of Theologicall and Phylosophicall Truth and perfect Piety
observations.note: What Paracelsus's divine writings tried to make known is set apart as one thing.

observations.quote: taken out of the Book of Grace and Nature, that is, that our mind should be raised up to God, and our eyes lifted up to look after the Truth
observations.note: The text says ('that is') what the Fundamentall comes to: the mind raised to God, the eyes to Truth, and a desire of blessedness 'through the Regeneration'.

observations.quote: Numen & Lumen, Divine Power and Light, these two make a perfect Man.
observations.note: Two Latin words with their English, 'Divine Power and Light', which together make a perfect man.

observations.quote: When the Light of Nature is well known, God or the Divine power of Grace is well known also.
observations.note: Knowing the Light of Nature well brings knowing God or 'the Divine power of Grace'.

observations.quote: By meditating or contemplating we know, by knowing we are delighted, by delighting we adhere, by adhearing we possesse, by possessing we injoy the Truth
observations.what: meditating, knowing, delighting, adhering, possessing, enjoying
observations.note: A graded chain of steps from meditating to enjoying the Truth, 'the food of our soules'.

observations.name: Div. Dionys.
observations.quote: Read Div. Dionys.
observations.note: The margin tells the reader to read named writers (the second name, Picus, is broken by gaps) and adds a Scripture place.

observations.quote: Without Phylosophy it is impossible to be absolutely godly; nor shall any man be ever able compleatly and Christianly to Phylosophize in either Light, who is not truely godly
observations.note: Godliness and Phylosophy are each made a condition of the other.

observations.quote: The two Lights are well known, within which are all thing, without which is nothing
observations.note: The two Lights, of Grace and of Nature, are set apart as holding all things and all perfect knowledge.

observations.quote: The Light of Grace, begetteth a true Theologer, yet not without Phylosophy
observations.note: The Light of Grace is described by what it produces: a true Theologer.

observations.quote: The Light of Nature, which is the Treasury of God confirmed in the Scriptures, maketh a true Phylosopher
observations.note: The Light of Nature is called 'the Treasury of God confirmed in the Scriptures' and makes a true Phylosopher. At CH5.1 the same name stood beside 'the liberty of human ingenuity'.

observations.quote: The works of God are bipactite; Philosophy comprehendeth the works or way of Nature; Theologie onely knoweth the works and way of Christ
observations.note: God's works are 'bipactite' (so spelled); Philosophy and Theologie each take one half.

observations.quote: In these two wayes we are to walk and spend our short time, that we may die in Peace and Joy.
observations.note: Both ways are to be walked.

observations.quote: every true Theologer is a Phylosopher, and every true Phylosopher is a Theologer
observations.note: The conclusion drawn ('Hence it is plaine'): the two callings coincide.

observations.quote: After Paracelsus others attempted this study, following the same strait and compendious tract
observations.what: others after Paracelsus who attempted this study
observations.note: A line of followers after Paracelsus is announced.

observations.quote: such as Paulus Brawn of Norimberge, Valentinus Weigelius, and Petrus Winzius
observations.what: Paulus Brawn of Norimberge, Valentinus Weigelius, and Petrus Winzius
observations.note: Three men are named as those followers; no words of theirs are given.

observations.quote: not in the sensuall school of fools, nor in the rationall school of Schollers, but in the third school of perfect Men, that Mentall or Intellectuall school of Pentecost
observations.what: the third school of perfect Men, that Mentall or Intellectuall school of Pentecost
observations.note: Three schools are told apart and numbered: sensual, rational, and the third, the 'school of Pentecost'.

observations.quote: all truly learned men walking in the Life and steps of Christ, have been taught and learned without labour and toyle
observations.note: In that school prophets, apostles and the truly learned are taught 'without labour and toyle'.

observations.quote: will in their time come to Light, unlesse the indignity and ingratitude of the world keep them back
observations.note: The manuscripts these men left are not yet in the open: they 'will in their time come to Light' unless the world's ingratitude keeps them back.

observations.quote: who yet are with-held in this hell of the body, under the yoak of misery
observations.note: The body is called a 'hell' in which readers' minds are held: a figure.

observations.quote: the annihilation, abnegation, immolation and mortification of themselves by Christ, casting all shadows behind them, and turning inward unto themselves into the Temple of the heart
observations.note: The practice is given as steps: after knowledge and lament of the Fall and daily contemplation, self-mortification and a turning inward 'into the Temple of the heart'. A practice of piety, not a work on a material.

observations.quote: by a daily practice of Piety fetch out that huge Talent and Treasury which is hid and shut up within themselvs
observations.note: A 'Talent and Treasury' is hidden and shut up within the readers, to be fetched out by daily piety.

observations.quote: like miserable mortall men who know not themselves, and consequently nothing else, lazily neglecting God within themselves
observations.note: Not knowing oneself is knowing nothing; such men neglect 'God within themselves'.

observations.quote: should in vaine seek those things without them by many books, mortall masters, long journeys, with great and constant paines, study and wearinesse
observations.note: Seeking outwardly, by books, masters and journeys, what one has within is called vain.

observations.quote: should in vaine seek those things without them by many books, mortall masters, long journeys
observations.note: Books and masters are here a vain way to what lies within; at CH5.4 no book is so bad 'but hath some good in it', and at CH5.3 other men's inventions are not to be slighted. 'Those things' here is the inward treasure, so the passages may speak of different things; recorded as a difference only.

observations.quote: The more we seek after things without us, the more we forget and loose our selves
observations.note: Outward seeking loses the self.

observations.name: 1 John 2.20, 27
observations.note: The margin lists Scripture places beside the passage on seeking within (more follow); no words of them are given.

observations.quote: God is to be waited for with a quiet mind when the sences are laid asleep
observations.note: God is waited for with a quiet mind, the senses 'laid asleep'.

observations.quote: Christ is to be found in the Temple of the Heart.
observations.note: The margin places Christ in 'the Temple of the Heart', repeating the inward search.

observations.quote: the whole Animall Man, who is nothing but EARTH
observations.note: The 'Animall Man' is said to be 'nothing but EARTH' (capitals in the text); to him the readers are to be dead.

observations.quote: supprest by the Sabbath and oblivion of Temporall things
observations.note: 'Sabbath' is joined with 'oblivion of Temporall things'. Interpreted (inference from that pairing): a rest from temporal things, not a day; the text does not say so itself.

observations.name: David, Psal. 40 1
observations.quote: entred into themselves with David, Psal. 40 1. patiently waiting for God our master who dwelleth in his holy Temple
observations.note: David and a Psalm are named for the inward waiting on God; the words are not marked as David's own.

observations.quote: in the Abysse of the heart or inward parts of our Soule, Psal. 5.7.
observations.note: God's 'holy Temple' is placed: 'the Abysse of the heart or inward parts of our Soule', with a Psalm cited.

observations.quote: which is the utmost happinesse and Blessednesse of Man, and the very determinate and appointed End of the Cabala or secret wisdome
observations.what: the very determinate and appointed End of the Cabala or secret wisdome
observations.note: God enlightening the mind and working 'all our works in us' is named man's utmost blessedness and the appointed End of the Cabala.

observations.quote: the Cabala or secret wisdome
observations.note: 'Cabala' is glossed by 'or secret wisdome'.

observations.quote: unhappy, foolish and miserable men had rather abide in themselves to their greatest damage and detriment of their right, then to be happy and wise in God
observations.note: A lament: men prefer to abide in themselves, not in God.

observations.quote: The heart of a Regenerate man is Gods Eden or Garden of Pleasure, wherein he dwelleth
observations.note: The regenerate heart is called God's Eden, his dwelling.

observations.quote: God made the World and Man that he might dwell in them as in his own proper house or Temple
observations.note: World and man were made as God's house or Temple.

observations.quote: though now he is not discerned by reason of the Dark Point of the Quaternary
observations.note: God is not now discerned 'by reason of the Dark Point of the Quaternary'; these lines do not say what that is.

observations.quote: at the end of this world which is to be Renewed by the Ternary of Man
observations.note: The renewal of the world is tied to 'the Ternary of Man', set against the Quaternary; 'Soul, Spirit, and Body' follow after the note mark.

observations.name: Apoc. 21.23
observations.note: The margin cites a Scripture place beside the passage on the New Jerusalem.

observations.quote: the Regeneration according to Soul, Spirit, and Body (the New Jerusalem, wherein the Unitrine Essence of God and the Holy and most Holy Trinity inseperably dwell)
observations.note: The Regeneration is threefold, by Soul, Spirit and Body, and is called in the parenthesis 'the New Jerusalem'.

observations.quote: will sparkle and glitter out with a radiant fiery colour like a Rubie or Carbuncle thorow the clear, spotlesse, beautifull body
observations.note: The Regeneration is said to shine through the body 'like a Rubie or Carbuncle': a comparison the text marks with 'like'.

observations.quote: in whom as in a Bodily Angel God himselfe is the Man, in the Temple of whose incontanimate mind God is the Ghest
observations.note: The blessed man is one in whom God dwells as guest, 'as in a Bodily Angel'.

observations.quote: where Mans Left hand knoweth not what Gods Right hand doth
observations.note: A turn of phrase, left unexplained in these lines, for God's working in such a man.

observations.quote: Unto this God the one and onely scope and end of all mens eyes should look
observations.note: God is the one aim all should look to.

observations.quote: all is vanity but to love God and cleave to him by serving him alone, and so to be united to the true Being by an humble subjection
observations.note: All is vanity except loving and serving God and being united 'to the true Being'.

observations.quote: we should slide into our selves or the Creatures as claiming to our selves the property both of them and of our selves
observations.note: The danger named: through disobedience, a proud will and self-love, to slide into oneself or the creatures.

observations.quote: fall back into that vaine, wicked or our own Nothing
observations.note: The end of that sliding is called 'our own Nothing'.

observations.quote: The Creature is ju{G170: 1 letter illegible}ily oblidged to obey the Creator, that our will may be one with God.
observations.note: The creature owes obedience so that the will be one with God; a Scripture place follows (one word holds a gap).

observations.quote: The Fall of Man and our great evill is to depart from Unity to Alterity.
observations.note: The margin says what the Fall is: departing 'from Unity to Alterity'.

observations.name: Seneca
observations.quote: I never go abroad among men but I come home lesse a man then when I went forth
observations.note: The margin gives a saying under Seneca's name.

observations.quote: If the Soule run back within it selfe and be converted into the Mind it draweth near to God, seeth all things, and hath no need of outward teaching
observations.note: The Soul turned into 'the Mind' nears God, sees all and needs no outward teaching, 'like the Angells'.

observations.quote: But when the Soule turneth into sence it is carried far off from God and departeth from God, the impure forsaketh the pure.
observations.note: The Soul turned to sense departs from God.

observations.quote: The Academicall spirit cannot not understand this Mystery; for Holy and Devout Humility alone, the most noble of all vertues, is capable of Illumination.
observations.note: The Mystery is closed to 'the Academicall spirit' and open to humility alone ('cannot not' stands so in the text).

observations.quote: this Truth cannot be comprehended except our Understanding be kindled by the Word of the Lord, and our Reason receive the Divine Light through the Mind
observations.note: The Truth is comprehended only by an understanding kindled by the Word and a reason lit through the Mind.

observations.quote: O what pains doe they take to become sools, who once drown themselves in Humane wisdome.
observations.note: An exclamation against those drowned in human wisdom ('sools' stands so).

observations.quote: nor may I in this unfit place openly speak more of these Mysteries
observations.note: Croll says he may not speak openly of these Mysteries here: something withheld by the author's own statement.

observations.quote: I returne againe to that Physitian Paracelsus from the digression unto which I had occasion to step aside
observations.note: The text calls what went before a digression and marks its return to Paracelsus (an earlier return stands at CH5.14).

observations.quote: It had been more becoming our Physitians to have extolld and huggd those great gifts of God in him
observations.note: The physicians ought to have honoured God's gifts in Paracelsus.

observations.quote: then to hate him for some kind of behaviour and using such words which every one doth not understand
observations.note: Paracelsus is hated for his behaviour and for 'words which every one doth not understand'.

observations.quote: tis easier to carp at him then to imitate him.
observations.note: Carping is easier than imitating; the margin note beside it (N214) holds foreign script given only as gaps.

observations.quote: tis easier to carp at him then to imitate him.
observations.note: Here imitating Paracelsus is hard but spoken of as the better course; N207 says 'it is impossible for any to imitate him'. Recorded as a difference in wording between text and margin.

observations.quote: The age wherein he wrote may excuse the harshnesse of his language, the malicious ingratitude of men may be the cause of the bewayled obscurity of his Commentators
observations.note: Two excuses: his age for his harsh language, men's ingratitude for the 'obscurity of his Commentators'.

observations.quote: the unusuall custome of Phylosophers plead for the strange novelties of names
observations.note: The strange new names are put down to the custom of philosophers.

observations.quote: the Phylosophers have ever driven from their hives of most sacred Sciences those sluggish and lazy Drones who are good for nothing but to devoure other mens industry
observations.note: The reason given for that custom: philosophers have always kept the idle ('Drones') away from the sciences ('hives').

observations.name: Plato
observations.quote: Arts wrapt in Riddles safe doe lye
observations.note: The couplet is given to Plato ('for as Plato saith,' at the end of CH5.25).

observations.quote: Their fruitfull'st soyle is Secrecy.
observations.note: The quoted verse says arts lie safe wrapped in riddles and grow best in secrecy.

observations.name: Plato
observations.quote: Artes ut lateant sua perque Aenigmata crescunt.
observations.note: The margin gives a Latin line beside the couplet given to Plato; the note names no one.

observations.quote: A man may live any where, Lawes and Liberties are alowed in every Dominion
observations.note: A general remark before the question that follows; its bearing is not spelled out in these lines.

observations.quote: let any man look into himselfe and consider if he had that which Theophrastus knew, whether he would tell it to every man
observations.note: The reader is asked whether he would himself tell everyone what Theophrastus knew: a defence of withholding.

observations.name: Hippocrates
observations.quote: in so doing he would break the Oath of Hippocrates, who would not instruct every one in the Art of Physick
observations.note: The Oath of Hippocrates is named as forbidding the teaching of physick to everyone; no words of it are given.

observations.quote: whether he would tell it to every man
observations.note: Here what Theophrastus knew is not to be told to every man; at CH5.12 he 'knew and publisht such hard and hidden secrets', and N197 says all secrets are by divine ordination to be discovered. Recorded as a difference, not judged.

dropped.reason: The quote shows writings left behind, not a hiding; the withholding of those manuscripts is kept from A95 and B136.

voices.quote: I think and judge as cause I finde
voices.basis: CH5.1 ends 'alwayes remembring that of Horace,'
Latin lines in the margin of the verse given to Horace; the note itself names no one

voices.quote: all sects, be they never so many
voices.basis: 'as said that most noble and wise Picus Mirandula'

voices.quote: and because knowledge thriveth as ingenuity is improved
voices.basis: runs on from the words given to Fabius; no mark shows where his words end
'acording to the conclusion of Hippocrates & Galen'

voices.quote: let him be the legetimate INTERPRETER of NATURE
voices.basis: 'as Paracelsus saith'; the margin N199 names 'Chirurgia magna'

voices.quote: Phylosophy teacheth the vertues and qualityes
voices.basis: follows straight on the words given to Paracelsus in CH5.8, in the same manner of instruction, with no mark of where his words end

voices.quote: as though the wicked one were the worker of those cures
voices.basis: view of 'they' (the Devil's 'Emissaries and catch-poles', CH5.14) reported in order to be rejected; no words of theirs given

voices.quote: I never go abroad among men
voices.basis: the note ends with the name 'Seneca'

voices.quote: Arts wrapt in Riddles safe doe lye

voices.basis: Latin line in the margin of the verse given to Plato; the note names no one
